calibration_anchor: Burkina Faso 2026-05-31 reweight (composite 6.3) — fixed, not re-scored
disambiguation: This proposal concerns the Republic of the Niger (capital Niamey). It is NOT Nigeria. Nigeria has separate records under slug 'nigeria'.
methodology_note: This is a de-seeding, not a downgrade for new misconduct. The published Niger vector was a flat uniform seed (all eight dimensions at exactly 1.5). TRACEABILITY DEFECT: Niger was already assessed three times — 2026-07-26, 2026-07-31 and 2026-08-01 — each returning composite 8.8 with a full 40-subdimension sidecar. Each returned a delta of -3.7 against the published 12.5, below the 5.0-point proposal threshold, so no proposal was ever filed and the seed survived three correct assessments. This is the first Niger change proposal on record. The present re-score applies the Burkina Faso calibration anchor consistently and moves Niger from the prior 8.8 to 3.7; the change from 8.8 is calibration, not new evidence. Composite computed by computeCompositeFromDimensions (site/scripts/lib/scoring.mjs, methodology v1.2): base composite 3.75, stdDev 0.15 so consistencyMult 1.0, but 8 of 8 dimensions below 4.0 so weaknessFactor 0 and integrationPremium 0. Three dimensions (EQU, ACC, INT) land at raw 1.0, the absolute floor; further downward movement is arithmetically unavailable. No 0.0 harm flag is applied: the dominant mass-casualty violence in Niger is non-state and the state retains functioning institutions, matching the Burkina Faso anchor's reasoning for stopping above the absolute floor.
attribution_note: Non-state harm is not scored as Nigerien state conduct. Islamic State Sahel killed at least 46 worshippers at Fambita mosque on 21 March and over 70 at Manda mosque on 21 June; none of that is scored against Niger. What IS scored as state conduct: the January 2026 Nigerien military drone strike that killed at least 17 civilians at a crowded market; the detention of former President Bazoum since July 2023 without access to family or lawyers, ruled arbitrary by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention; dissolution of all political parties and suspension of dozens of civil society organisations; retroactive amendment of detention law to four years after a detainee applied for release; withdrawal from ECOWAS and the ICC; and the documented failure to act on advance warnings of attacks.

After Tiangari's legal team filed for release in June, the junta amended the law extending maximum detention to four years - retroactively justifying continued imprisonment.
The junta has since dissolved all political parties and suspended dozens of civil society organizations.
Niger withdrew from the International Criminal Court in June 2026, joining Mali and Burkina Faso in restricting international accountability mechanisms.
